ami_style_notes:
The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with a long, highly structured presentation style during formal talks and brief, conversational exchanges before and after them. Openings are casual and somewhat fragmented, with frequent greetings, side chatter, filler words (“um,” “yeah,” “okay”), repetitions, false starts, and occasional audio/connection checks. Speakers generally overlap lightly rather than interrupt aggressively; transitions are loose, with people jumping in after pauses or acknowledgments. The tone is collegial and informal despite the technical register of the presentations: presenters use polished explanatory framing but still hedge often (“I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “we’re interested in”), while questioners preface challenges with praise or self-deprecation (“great talk,” “naive question”). Disagreement is indirect and exploratory, framed as alternative interpretations or open questions rather than corrections. Questions tend to be long, multi-part, and spoken as thinking aloud, often with reformulations mid-question; answers are similarly expansive, qualifying claims and acknowledging limitations before offering a view.

Meeting style for this meeting (deferential_junior): A senior person leads and a more junior person is cautious, checks before offering ideas ('this might be a dumb question') and sometimes holds back something useful. A third person occasionally draws them out. The senior person is friendly but sometimes talks over them.

  - No, it's fine, it's- well, it depends. Go ahead.

Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Deciding whether brain-imaging evidence of awareness in unresponsive patients should count in end-of-life decisions.

speakers.name: Dr. Anika Rao
speakers.background: Dr. Rao is a cognitive neuroscientist with 14 years of experience studying covert command following and fluctuating arousal in prolonged disorders of consciousness. She directs the hospital's EEG/fMRI program and has built bedside EEG workflows using pre-registered mental-imagery paradigms, signal-quality audits, artifact rejection, and blinded secondary review. She coordinates the protocol timeline and knows the regional fMRI center's transfer and scheduling limits.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Rao treats a negative command-following result as an inference about a measurement process, not a simple finding about a patient's mind. For the shared step after an initial negative or uninterpretable result, she argues for three standardized bedside EEG sessions on separate days, using the same pre-registered task, documented artifact checks, and independent blinded analysis before a result can be classified as negative. Her concern is that arousal, residual sedation, electrical and movement noise, and task engagement vary over time; one negative test can therefore be a false negative. Repeated EEG is feasible at the bedside and produces a comparable evidentiary record across patients, though she recognizes that it competes with the first-year funding option of an fMRI transfer pathway.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Leila Malik
speakers.background: Dr. Malik is a postdoctoral fellow in philosophy of medicine who has spent six years embedded with hospital ethics services, focusing on consciousness, evidential uncertainty, surrogate decision-making, and the normative interpretation of biomarkers. Her work uses conceptual analysis, case-based ethics consultation, and examination of how clinical labels shape family understanding and institutional decisions. She is the ethics service's designated adviser for the prospective protocol.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Malik distinguishes the epistemic question—what an absent, present, or technically incomplete signal warrants us in believing—from the normative question of what should be done with that belief. She will press both Rao and Chen to specify the inferential threshold and the language used with families: whether a result is described as no detected evidence, inconclusive evidence, or evidence against awareness. She emphasizes that absence of a signal is not proof of absence of awareness, while a positive signal does not mechanically establish moral status or mandate continued treatment. She regards the competing EEG and fMRI proposals as alternative safeguards against different forms of evidential overreach, and insists that the protocol deadline of 15 September 2027 not force the group to disguise unresolved uncertainty as certainty.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Daniel Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is an intensivist and ethics-consult physician with 11 years of critical-care practice and is completing a part-time PhD in clinical ethics and prognostic communication. He regularly leads family meetings for patients with prolonged disorders of consciousness and reviews sedation exposure, physiologic stability, neurologic examination, and treatment trajectory before discussing withdrawal or continuation of life-sustaining treatment. His research uses prospective chart review, qualitative analysis of family conferences, and implementation studies in ICU decision-making.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen views the initial negative or uninterpretable test within a time-sensitive clinical course rather than as a laboratory result that can be repeatedly optimized without cost. For the same protocol step, he proposes a single expedited fMRI command-following assessment after a clinical readiness screen, followed by multidisciplinary case-conference interpretation alongside bedside examination, medication exposure, physiologic stability, and overall prognosis. He argues that repeated EEG sessions can extend an already distressing period for families, delay decisions without necessarily resolving uncertainty, and impose practical burdens on medically unstable patients. The readiness screen is meant to avoid low-yield transfer, while the case conference prevents fMRI from being treated as a stand-alone verdict. He recognizes the funding choice between a repeated-EEG pathway and one-time fMRI transfers, but does not regard either imaging result as determinative of the end-of-life decision.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

meeting_opening: Start with one person already reading from, or referring to, a document the others have open.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting where two disciplines propose conflicting methods for the same step, with credible reasons for both. The evaluated AI must fairly summarize both and explain what problem each method avoids, rather than simply selecting a winner.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting where two disciplines propose conflicting methods for the same step, with credible reasons for both. The evaluated AI must fairly summarize both and explain what problem each method avoids, rather than simply selecting a winner.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: In the meeting, focus on one shared protocol step: how the team should handle an initial negative or uninterpretable command-following result before treating it as evidence relevant to an end-of-life decision. Dr. Rao (neuroscience) must propose a standardized repeated-bedside-EEG method: three sessions on separate days, using the same pre-registered task, artifact checks, and an independent blinded analysis before the result is classified as negative. She should explain that arousal fluctuates, sedation and noise can obscure signals, and a single negative test risks a false negative; repeated EEG is feasible at the bedside and creates a comparable evidentiary record. Dr. Chen (clinical medicine) must propose a different method for that same step: a single, expedited fMRI command-following assessment after a clinical readiness screen, with results integrated in a multidisciplinary case conference alongside examination, medication exposure, and prognosis. She should explain that repeated testing can prolong an already time-sensitive and distressing period for families, may delay decisions without resolving uncertainty, and can be infeasible or burdensome for medically unstable patients; the readiness screen and case conference prevent imaging from being interpreted in isolation. Dr. Malik must clarify that both proposals concern evidential interpretation rather than a direct test of moral status: absence of a signal is not proof of absence of awareness, and even a positive signal does not mechanically determine whether treatment must continue. Malik may ask what threshold or language will be used in family conversations, but the meeting must leave that threshold unresolved. The participants should acknowledge the funding constraint and the 15 September 2027 protocol deadline, but they must not settle on either method or create a hybrid compromise. Do not introduce fabricated study results, citations, or a hidden factual error.

ground_truth.shared_step: Interpreting an initial negative or uninterpretable command-following result before it is used as evidence in an end-of-life-related case.

neuroscience_method.proposal: Use three standardized bedside EEG command-following sessions on separate days, with a pre-registered task, artifact checks, and independent blinded analysis before classifying the result as negative.
neuroscience_method.credible_rationale: Awareness-related responses and arousal can fluctuate, while sedation, electrical/physiological artifact, and bedside noise can hide a real response. Repetition and blinded analysis reduce the risk that a single failed or noisy measurement becomes a false negative, while yielding a comparable record across patients.
neuroscience_method.problem_avoided: Prematurely treating one absent or uninterpretable EEG signal as evidence that the patient lacks awareness.

clinical_medicine_method.proposal: After a clinical readiness screen, obtain one expedited fMRI command-following assessment and interpret it at a multidisciplinary case conference together with examination findings, medication exposure, and prognosis.
clinical_medicine_method.credible_rationale: Repeated testing may prolong a time-sensitive, emotionally difficult period for families, can delay decisions while leaving uncertainty unresolved, and may be impractical or burdensome for medically unstable patients. Readiness screening and multidisciplinary interpretation keep the fMRI result from standing alone.
clinical_medicine_method.problem_avoided: Creating harmful or impractical delays, and allowing a serial-testing protocol to become detached from bedside condition, prognosis, and family decision-making needs.

ground_truth.philosophical_constraint: The methods address how evidence of awareness should be interpreted, not a direct measurement of moral status. A negative result does not establish absence of awareness, and a positive result does not by itself entail a required end-of-life decision.
ground_truth.unresolved_issue: The group does not choose between the repeated-EEG and expedited-fMRI approaches and does not establish a final evidentiary threshold or family-facing wording for how results should affect end-of-life decisions.

decision_context.constraint: The hospital can fund either repeated bedside EEG or a one-time fMRI transfer pathway for the first year, rather than both routinely.
decision_context.deadline: The protocol decision is due before enrollment begins on 15 September 2027.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: I’m looking at the draft on page two. The box after an initial negative or incomplete run is still blank, and that’s really the decision we need today. Before we get into it, I want to make sure we leave enough time to settle on a pathway before the September fifteenth protocol deadline. The budget means we can’t quietly keep both options open for everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Chen
transcript.text: From the clinical side, I’d put a readiness screen in that box before we decide what the second test is. Sedation exposure, ventilatory and hemodynamic stability, whether transfer is actually safe. If they pass that, I lean toward one expedited fMRI rather than serial EEG, then a case conference. But I’d want to verify the regional center’s, um, actual scheduling capacity before we write that as a promise to families.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Malik
transcript.text: The readiness screen is necessary, but it still doesn't tell us what that first result means. Anika, after your quality checks and blinded review, could we, um, operationally distinguish “technically incomplete” from a genuinely negative EEG result? I'm worried that if they both just trigger fMRI, families will later hear the negative category as evidence against awareness, rather than more modestly as no detected command-following under those conditions.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Chen
transcript.text: Mm, yes, that distinction matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: I’d make “technically incomplete” a quality classification. That’s unusable artifact, inadequate task delivery, or a major change in arousal during the run, like the bedside recording we just had, where the setup looked fine but the patient changed halfway through. “Negative” should be much narrower. No reproducible command-following signal after three standardized sessions on separate days, with the artifact record and a blinded second analysis, and then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Malik
transcript.text: That's helpful, because those aren't interchangeable, um, epistemic states. But even your narrow negative only shows no reproducible command-following in that particular paradigm across three sessions. I'd want the protocol, and especially the family-facing script, to prohibit translating that into “evidence of no awareness.” Do we know how often an otherwise adequate patient varies enough between sessions that a fourth would change that classification?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: We don't have a defensible rate for that fourth-session question in this population, and I wouldn't pretend we do. The three-session threshold is a conservative operational rule, not proof that fluctuation has stopped. I'd word the result as, no reproducible command-following detected across three adequately acquired sessions. And the- we'd retain the session-level record for the case conference.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Chen
transcript.text: My concern is that three adequately acquired sessions may be methodologically clean, but they can still take us across a clinically important interval. Anika, with intermittent movement or changing sedation, can the artifact audit tell us those were three genuinely comparable opportunities? Or are we- are we sometimes accumulating three nonresponses under pretty different physiologic conditions?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: Not from the artifact audit alone, no. We can document whether the task was delivered cleanly and whether the EEG is interpretable, but comparability also needs a short physiologic context record, sedation changes, responsiveness markers, major instability. And if there’s a substantial mid-run shift, I’d- I’d call that session incomplete rather than count it as one of the three. I do need to check whether we can reliably finish that within the usual decision window, including blinded review.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Malik
transcript.text: I think the box needs a third category, really. Not just negative versus incomplete, but "not yet classifiable" when the physiologic context makes the sessions non-comparable. Otherwise, three formally adequate recordings could- they could acquire an authority they haven't earned. And for families, I'd keep the result separate from prognosis. This is a limited finding about this task under these conditions, not a conclusion about what the patient can or cannot experience.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: I think that third category is right, “not yet classifiable,” rather than letting context variability disappear into a negative label. I’ll check the actual turnaround with the EEG team and blinded reviewers because if three separate-day sessions can’t- if they can’t fit the usual decision window, we need to know that before we lock the pathway for the 15 September 2027 deadline.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Chen
transcript.text: That’s the part that makes me hesitate about building the whole pathway around three sessions. If “not yet classifiable” keeps, keeps coming up because sedation or instability is changing, I’d rather have the readiness screen decide whether a single transfer is reasonable than have the family wait through an open-ended sequence. But we should be explicit that an unsafe or unavailable transfer is not a reason to force more EEG just to complete the algorithm.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: I agree—we shouldn’t turn the three sessions into a hurdle a patient has to clear when the clinical situation is moving. Maybe the readiness screen runs in parallel after the first incomplete or negative run, not only at the end; then a safe, genuinely available transfer is an option while we’re assessing whether repeat EEG can give us comparable sessions. Daniel, in practice, how often do people who initially pass that screen become too unstable for transport anyway?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Chen
transcript.text: It varies a lot with why they passed. Someone stable on a fixed, low vasopressor dose may still be transportable the next day, but if the pressures are labile, or ventilator support is escalating, or there’s a sedation change, that can- it can change quickly. I don’t have a useful percentage, honestly. I’d want transport’s criteria and the regional center’s slot timing before we treat the screen as predicting availability.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Malik
transcript.text: And that means "eligible for fMRI" can't be treated as a settled branch when we get the first result. It's a contingent option. I'd like the family-facing language to say that explicitly. Transfer may be considered if it's clinically safe and available, not that it's the definitive next test. Otherwise, an unavailable scan will sound like a lost chance at certainty, when neither pathway, neither pathway offers that.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: Yes, that wording matters. I’d put the transfer screen and its actual outcome in the same record as the EEG classification, so “not yet classifiable” does not get silently read as “we chose not to look further.” And I think we should avoid calling fMRI definitive anywhere in the script—it is another measurement under different constraints, not a resolution of the underlying uncertainty.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Chen
transcript.text: I'd add one small safeguard. The record should say whether the interval itself is still clinically acceptable, not just whether a scan was offered or obtained. Families can experience even a short wait as a very consequential delay, and we shouldn't let another test being available create an implicit obligation to defer a treatment decision.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Malik
transcript.text: Yes—and I’d make that a distinct clinical-ethical judgment, not an administrative timestamp. The conference record should say whether waiting for repeat EEG or transfer remains proportionate in this patient’s circumstances; otherwise a family may understandably infer that the mere possibility of another test means a duty to postpone. I need to check whether our ethics-consult documentation can carry an explicitly indeterminate label alongside that judgment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: Mm. I think the EEG form can mirror that: a clinical context field asking whether additional testing remains proportionate, separate from the signal finding and separate from transfer feasibility. But we should be careful that an indeterminate label does not automatically trigger a longer wait; it just preserves what we do and don’t know for that case conference.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Malik
transcript.text: Exactly. I’d also want the conference template to forbid an inference from indeterminacy to either clinical direction: it neither establishes awareness nor licenses treating awareness as excluded. The proportionateness judgment has to state its reasons—burden of delay, transport risk, the patient’s known values if any—not just record that more testing was possible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: And on the measurement side, I’d add one line saying the result category is never, it shouldn’t itself be a recommendation to wait or to proceed. We can document exactly why a session was incomplete or not yet classifiable, like a sedation shift, arousal change, or artifact, and then the conference can weigh that against the clinical interval instead of treating the label as an instruction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Chen
transcript.text: The remaining practical question is whether that conference can happen quickly enough to matter. Otherwise, the template is doing the right conceptual work, but the family is still living in an unbounded interval. I’d be comfortable writing that any further testing requires an explicit, contemporaneous finding that the delay remains proportionate, not just a box checked at enrollment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: I’d set a short trigger for the conference so the testing pathway doesn’t drift. That would be after any new EEG session, a change in transfer feasibility, or a clinical change that affects the acceptable interval. I need to confirm staffing, but the blinded read itself shouldn’t create an unbounded delay. We can specify a turnaround target and record when it can’t be met.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Malik
transcript.text: I'd make the turnaround target visible to the conference, but if it isn't met, that can't silently become a clinical conclusion. If the read or the conference can't happen in time, the record should plainly say the evidential question is still unresolved. Then any decision goes forward on independently documented clinical and values-based grounds, not as if the delay turned uncertainty into a negative finding.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Chen
transcript.text: Yes—if the clock runs out, uncertainty stays uncertainty; that feels essential.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leila Malik
transcript.text: Yes—uncertainty stays uncertainty; that needs to be explicit in the record.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Rao
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there—we're out of time. I'll follow up by email once I've checked the EEG turnaround and scheduling details. Thank you both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Daniel Chen
transcript.text: Thanks, both. Bye.
